name: Bellman equation for v_π

symbols.meaning: chance that policy π selects action a when in state s
probability of next state s′ and reward r after action a in state s
discount rate
value of the successor state under π

intuition: Look one step ahead: the value of s is the probability-weighted average, over every action, next state and reward, of the reward plus the discounted value of where you land.
assumptions: Actions range over A(s); next states over S (or S+ for episodic tasks); rewards over R.
The environment has the Markov property, so p(s′, r | s, a) describes the dynamics completely.

derivation.why: Write the return as the discounted sum of rewards.
Separate the first reward and factor γ out of the rest.
Expand the expectation over the first action, next state and reward; by the Markov property the rest depends only on S_{t+1} = s′.
The inner expectation is v_π(s′); merge the two sums over s′ and r.

example: In Example 4.1 (γ = 1, reward −1 everywhere, four equally likely moves) state 1 (left: terminal, up: stays in 1, right: 2, down: 5) satisfies $v_\pi(1) = -1 + \tfrac14\big(v_\pi(T) + v_\pi(1) + v_\pi(2) + v_\pi(5)\big) = -1 + \tfrac14(0 - 14 - 20 - 18) = -14$.
significance: Turned into an assignment it becomes the update of iterative policy evaluation (4.5).
pitfalls: The terminal state has value 0; forgetting this breaks episodic examples.
Every (s′, r) pair is weighted by π(a|s)·p(s′, r|s, a), not by p alone.

verification.note: The worked example is checked by ch03.bellman-example-state-1.

name: Return as a plain sum of rewards

symbols.meaning: the return from time t
the final time step of the episode

intuition: Add up every reward still to come in the episode. This only makes sense when the interaction ends.
assumptions: The task is episodic: a final time step T exists.
example: An episode with rewards $0, 0, 1$ after time 0 has $G_0 = 1$, $G_1 = 1$ and $G_2 = 1$.
pitfalls: For a continuing task T would be ∞ and the sum could be infinite (a reward of +1 every step, for example).

verification.note: Printed p. 59 (PDF p. 73), checked on the page image.

name: Discounted return

symbols.meaning: the discount rate, 0 ≤ γ ≤ 1
the weight on the reward k + 1 steps ahead

intuition: Future rewards count less the further away they are. With γ < 1 a bounded reward sequence has a finite sum; γ = 0 makes the agent myopic, and γ near 1 makes it farsighted.
assumptions: γ < 1, or the episode terminates, so that the sum is defined.
significance: Almost every algorithm in the book estimates the expected value of this quantity.
pitfalls: A reward k steps in the future is worth γ^{k−1} of an immediate one: R_{t+1} carries weight γ⁰ = 1.
Maximising only the next reward (γ = 0) can reduce the return when actions affect later rewards.

verification.note: Printed p. 60 (PDF p. 74), checked on the page image.

name: Return for episodic and continuing tasks

symbols.meaning: the final time step, possibly ∞
the discount rate, possibly 1

intuition: Thanks to the absorbing state with zero rewards, one formula covers both kinds of task: stop at T for an episode, or run to infinity for a continuing task.
assumptions: T = ∞ or γ = 1 is allowed, but not both, so the sum stays finite.
pitfalls: With T = ∞ and γ = 1 together the return may be undefined; continuing undiscounted tasks need a different formulation.

verification.note: Printed p. 62 (PDF p. 76), checked on the page image. Checked numerically against (3.1) and (3.2) by ch03.absorbing-state-return.

flags.note: Footnote 6, attached to this equation, says some ideas on continuing undiscounted tasks are discussed in Section 11.2. In this draft §11.2 is 'Eligibility Traces for Actor–Critic Methods'; the average-reward setting is treated in §11.3, on R-learning and the average-reward setting (checked in the text layer).

name: Dynamics conditioned on the whole history

symbols.meaning: everything that happened before the current step

intuition: In the most general (causal) case, what happens next can depend on the entire past.
assumptions: Finitely many states and reward values, so probabilities rather than densities.
pitfalls: This is not a quantity the agent can compute; it is the benchmark a Markov state must match.

verification.note: Printed p. 64 (PDF p. 78), checked on the page image.

name: Dynamics of a Markov state
tex: p(s', r|s, a) = \Pr\{R_{t+1} = r, S_{t+1} = s' \mid S_t, A_t\}

symbols.meaning: the current state and action only

intuition: If the state is Markov, the current state and action already tell you everything the history could about the next state and reward.
assumptions: The state signal has the Markov property: (3.5) equals (3.4) for every history.
pitfalls: Markov does not mean deterministic: the next state can still be random.
Hidden information the agent never observed (the next card in a deck) does not stop a state from being Markov.

verification.note: Printed p. 64 (PDF p. 78), checked on the page image.

name: Dynamics of a finite MDP
tex: p(s', r|s, a) = \Pr\{S_{t+1} = s', R_{t+1} = r \mid S_t = s, A_t = a\}

symbols.meaning: the probability of next state s′ and reward r after action a in state s

intuition: One table of probabilities, indexed by state, action, next state and reward, specifies the whole environment.
assumptions: Finite state, action and reward sets.
The Markov property.
pitfalls: For each (s, a) the probabilities over all (s′, r) pairs sum to 1.

verification.note: Printed p. 67 (PDF p. 81), checked on the page image.

name: Expected reward for a state–action pair
tex: r(s, a) = \mathbb{E}[R_{t+1} \mid S_t = s, A_t = a] = \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} r \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} p(s', r|s, a)

symbols.meaning: the reward expected on taking a in s

intuition: Average the reward over every outcome, whatever the next state.
assumptions: The dynamics (3.6) are known.
pitfalls: In the recycling robot, searching in low gives β r_search + (1 − β)(−3), not r_search: the rescue penalty counts.

verification.note: Printed p. 67 (PDF p. 81), checked on the page image.

name: State-transition probabilities
tex: p(s'|s, a) = \Pr\{S_{t+1} = s' \mid S_t = s, A_t = a\} = \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} p(s', r|s, a)

symbols.meaning: the probability of moving to s′, whatever the reward

intuition: Sum the joint dynamics over the rewards to get where you land.
assumptions: The dynamics (3.6) are known.
pitfalls: The three-argument p(s′|s, a) loses the distribution of rewards; it cannot replace (3.6).

verification.note: Printed p. 67 (PDF p. 81), checked on the page image.

name: Expected reward for a transition
tex: r(s, a, s') = \mathbb{E}[R_{t+1} \mid S_t = s, A_t = a, S_{t+1} = s'] = \frac{\sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} r\, p(s', r|s, a)}{p(s'|s, a)}

symbols.meaning: the reward expected on a particular transition

intuition: Condition on the next state as well: of the outcomes that land in s′, what is the average reward?
assumptions: p(s′|s, a) > 0, or the quotient is undefined.
example: Searching in low and landing in high means the battery ran out: $r(\text{low}, \text{search}, \text{high}) = -3$ (Table 3.1).
pitfalls: Table 3.1 lists r(s, a, s′) even for zero-probability rows (e.g. waiting in high and landing in low); there the value is a convention, not a conditional expectation.

verification.note: Printed p. 67 (PDF p. 81), checked on the page image.

name: State-value function
tex: v_\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t \mid S_t = s] = \mathbb{E}_\pi\Big[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k R_{t+k+1} \,\Big|\, S_t = s\Big]

symbols.meaning: expectation when the agent follows π
any time step

intuition: The value of a state is the return you expect if you start there and follow π.
assumptions: The expectation exists (γ < 1 or episodes end).
A terminal state has value 0.
pitfalls: Values belong to a policy: the same state has different values under different policies.

verification.note: Printed p. 70 (PDF p. 84), checked on the page image.

name: Action-value function
tex: q_\pi(s, a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t \mid S_t = s, A_t = a] = \mathbb{E}_\pi\Big[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k R_{t+k+1} \,\Big|\, S_t = s, A_t = a\Big]

symbols.meaning: the expected return after taking a in s and following π afterwards

intuition: Like v_π, but the first action is fixed rather than chosen by π.
assumptions: The first action a need not be one π would choose.
pitfalls: v_π(s) = Σ_a π(a|s) q_π(s, a) (Exercise 3.12); q_π is not the same as the immediate reward.

verification.note: Printed p. 70 (PDF p. 84), checked on the page image. The relations to v_π are checked numerically by ch03.bellman-q-pi.

name: Optimal state-value function

symbols.meaning: the optimal state-value function, shared by all optimal policies

intuition: The best value any policy can achieve from each state.
assumptions: A finite MDP, in which an optimal policy (better than or equal to all others in every state) exists.
pitfalls: The maximum is taken state by state, yet one policy attains it in every state at once.

verification.note: Printed p. 75 (PDF p. 89), checked on the page image.

name: Optimal action-value function

symbols.meaning: the expected return for taking a in s and then behaving optimally

intuition: The best you can expect after committing to a first action.
assumptions: A finite MDP.
pitfalls: q_*(s, a) can be below v_*(s): the first action may be a poor one.

verification.note: Printed p. 75 (PDF p. 89), checked on the page image.

name: q_* in terms of v_*
tex: q_*(s, a) = \mathbb{E}[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_*(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s, A_t = a]

symbols.meaning: the optimal value of the next state

intuition: Take the action, collect the reward, and from the next state on act optimally.
assumptions: The dynamics determine the expectation; no policy is needed for the first step.
example: In the 5 × 5 gridworld, below B (where $v_* \approx 17.80$), moving up into B gives $0 + 0.9 \times 19.42 = 17.48$, while moving left gives $0.9 \times 19.78 = 17.80$: left is optimal.
pitfalls: Expanding the expectation with the four-argument dynamics gives the answer to Exercise 3.19.

verification.note: Printed p. 75 (PDF p. 89), checked on the page image. Checked numerically by ch03.optimal-relations.

name: Bellman optimality equation for v_* (expectation form)
tex: v_*(s) = \max_a \mathbb{E}[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_*(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s, A_t = a]

symbols.meaning: over the actions available in s

intuition: A state's optimal value is the expected return of its best action.
assumptions: v_* is the value function of an optimal policy, so it satisfies (3.12) for that policy.

derivation.why: An optimal policy's value is that of its best action.
The rest is the return from S_{t+1} under an optimal policy, whose expectation is v_*(S_{t+1}).

pitfalls: The maximum replaces the policy's average over actions; there is no π left in the equation.

verification.note: Printed p. 76 (PDF p. 90), checked on the page image.

name: Bellman optimality equation for v_*
tex: v_*(s) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}(s)} \sum_{s', r} p(s', r|s, a)\big[r + \gamma v_*(s')\big]

symbols.meaning: the dynamics (3.6)

intuition: One equation per state, each taking the best action's expected reward plus discounted next value. Together they pin down v_* uniquely.
assumptions: A finite MDP with known dynamics.
γ < 1, or a setting in which the values are finite.
example: Recycling robot (Example 3.11): $v_*(\text{high}) = \max\{r_s + \gamma[\alpha v_*(\text{high}) + (1-\alpha) v_*(\text{low})],\ r_w + \gamma v_*(\text{high})\}$.
pitfalls: The system is nonlinear because of the max, so it is not solved like (3.12) by one linear solve.
Solving it exactly is rarely practical (§3.9).

verification.note: Printed p. 76 (PDF p. 90), checked on the page image. Its solution for the 5 × 5 gridworld reproduces Figure 3.8 (ch03.fig3-8-values).

name: Bellman optimality equation for q_*
tex: q_*(s, a) = \mathbb{E}\Big[R_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a'} q_*(S_{t+1}, a') \,\Big|\, S_t = s, A_t = a\Big] = \sum_{s', r} p(s', r|s, a)\Big[r + \gamma \max_{a'} q_*(s', a')\Big]

symbols.meaning: the best action in the next state

intuition: Same idea for action values: after the first action, the agent picks the best action every time.
assumptions: A finite MDP.
pitfalls: The max sits inside the sum, at the next state, not outside it as in (3.17).

verification.note: Printed unnumbered on p. 76 (PDF p. 90), checked on the page image. Checked numerically by ch03.optimal-relations.
